ready.title: nexus: research self-learning systems that refine agent communication
ready.body:
Captain 2026-10-05 06:36Z: 'I want you to have a research job, go out and basically look for really good examples of self-learning systems with regards to refining communication for agents. I feel like we're continuously saying the same thing to try to get you to behave in the same way, but is there some sort of self-learning guideline, guardrail feature, combination of options or tools or anything out there that we can use?' Questions: (1) systems or papers where an agent learns durable communication or behavior rules from user corrections (feedback memory, preference learning, rule distillation, reflection loops); (2) tools or frameworks usable with Claude Code, opencode or similar CLI agents (hooks, memory layers, guardrail libraries, evals that score replies against a style rubric); (3) how each enforces a rule after it is learned, not just stores it; (4) which fit a fleet where corrections arrive by chat and must reach every agent. Give citations, maturity, cost, and a ranked shortlist for us.

# Research Report

**Question:** nexus: research self-learning systems that refine agent communication

Captain 2026-10-05 06:36Z: 'I want you to have a research job, go out and basically look for really good examples of self-learning systems with regards to refining communication for agents. I feel like we're continuously saying the same thing to try to get you to behave in the same way, but is there some sort of self-learning guideline, guardrail feature, combination of options or tools or anything out there that we can use?' Questions: (1) systems or papers where an agent learns durable communication or behavior rules from user corrections (feedback memory, preference learning, rule distillation, reflection loops); (2) tools or frameworks usable with Claude Code, opencode or similar CLI agents (hooks, memory layers, guardrail libraries, evals that score replies against a style rubric); (3) how each enforces a rule after it is learned, not just stores it; (4) which fit a fleet where corrections arrive by chat and must reach every agent. Give citations, maturity, cost, and a ranked shortlist for us.

## Sub‑questions
1. What academic papers and production systems document LLM agents distilling durable behavioral or communication rules from user corrections (such as feedback memory, reflection loops, and rule distillation), and what are their citations and maturity levels?
2. What existing open-source libraries, memory layers, and guardrail frameworks (e.g., Letta/MemGPT, LangMem, NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI) can integrate with CLI-based agents like Claude Code or opencode via hooks, system prompt injection, or middleware?
3. What architectural mechanisms do surveyed systems use to actively enforce learned rules at runtime (e.g., dynamic prompt compilation, retrieval-augmented prompt patches, pre/post-generation rubric evaluators, or output validation) beyond passive storage?
4. What architectures or protocols exist for propagating user corrections and distilled communication rules across a multi-agent fleet from a centralized or shared data store (such as git-backed instruction files, shared vector/relational stores, or pub/sub sync)?
5. What is the ranked shortlist of candidate approaches and tools for the nexus project based on implementation complexity, operational cost, Python 3.10 compatibility, and effectiveness in preventing repetitive communication corrections?

## Draft
# Distilling durable behavioral/communication rules from user corrections: academic foundations, tooling, enforcement, fleet propagation, and cost

## 1. Academic papers and production systems

**Reflection / self-critique loops.** Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) converts task feedback into verbal self-reflections stored in an episodic buffer and reused on later attempts, improving behavior without weight updates; its limitation for nexus is that reflections are scoped to a single task episode, not promoted to durable cross-session rules. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) is the sibling work — iterative self-feedback within one generation — and is weaker still on durability since nothing persists past the response. `unverified: exact arXiv identifiers for Reflexion, Self-Refine, RLHF, Constitutional AI, Generative Agents, Voyager, MemGPT` — titles/authors/years are reliable, numeric IDs should be confirmed before citation. Web sources corroborate the reflection-loop pattern generally (Generate → Reflect/Critique → Refine, with reflections stored as "playbooks") [1](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQG-zWJfOemqIJWflRX6w3g_pweSyrvDaDGXfgQQtFUxS8WVlUxmLrypDz3cZFB05-EemJzuU8cNdiiAjyqb7KFd1r4B43LUb65bXMaiYI7vHZy315fNG2liB66fzFaemtRAOp8EBvTmZ8yVajKADhmv82wb8QTuOwj4Ig==) [2](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEFuOrhsjVmN3jDIXmCx10KzfTrZjTyzKNRjeuLIqnXgFYriPvLn7naqgmev_UznJfPXYm7n8rWUJdpiNsLplNNtQWSgl-ISWI3062LslYt9p4E6ljrMOxCxwPpqEsFjVkWOE57gyM=) [3](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQH9B46b4s4uENfl_NhcGGTG5A5_u6YDtG4YUmY1hfMnof38TOmu9HIJkadu7q5VFa7EQIxjcd4CmtOsu4Aa1WkYA4w5KtwABJP5jgV4r9JH9AiWrFKRMRF6WfWAh8H4FFmxppxlQmbGNS9cxd6jBgNcZ1mzix1iEmuRKg7SOg2xjveb12qMn_imhVtCNk9ckAevAjpW) [4](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHkf16ofSUT176kEqKahI6DCp3VBpELpnpRVVRX345q2zGqe4aC1T9yHNw_DN-77KdbdSGXxGDSxqR2v_-cybUuQIkCp0E3F47ahK5vHv-nKvJKWd75SdUoPolbzg6l56Wv-rclXJmtGX4Y_cLapr6B2XSTm_dpkyu2u4hikG92faGmfvnZ3He_Y09pkUVlPA9sQnZJ7zU=).

**Feedback memory / preference learning.** RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; InstructGPT, Ouyang et al., 2022) learns durable behavioral policy from human preference corrections, but at training time and model-owner scale — not runnable per-correction by a CLI fleet. The practically relevant branch is *in-context* preference learning: Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) shows rules expressed as explicit principles can govern generation, and Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) demonstrates a memory stream with reflection and retrieval producing durable, consistent behavior across sessions — the closest academic analogue to a persistent correction store. Web sources corroborate this branch: PRELUDE and CIPHER infer latent user preferences from edit histories without fine-tuning, aggregating feedback into a "preference policy" [5](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFL6KSdrvR_VbwQPGTns5RqR5dGF64OqRnOOfrwQoJP3rqMx1kZ25qg2t0Z4D_FOZNBYIpipilw-GvEN3RcLm6vWNpJaBZMtvkrumiM_inmyO14c-wT4xJ-AWIgy6jzrRg=), and MAPL extends this to multi-agent settings via comparative feedback [6](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFXtOVnz6XtQPf0JMkKQrCejru-Eek2x3oYNwzlyAC9Oaa7ZTm-Fy44zqm6f0Q9srdZjaWxxjr31WoArBANeBHuuuZlIt8kAywGyPFavt6758zvhtwJxw==).

**Rule distillation into durable artifacts.** Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) distills successful behavior into a reusable, growing skill library; MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) formalizes tiered memory with explicit write/eviction so learned facts persist across context windows. These are the papers whose mechanism (write a durable artifact, retrieve and apply it later) maps onto a fleet-wide rule store.

**Production systems.** LangChain/LangGraph memory modules and LangMem (persistent semantic/episodic/procedural memory with explicit update operations); Mem0 (open-source memory layer extracting and consolidating facts from conversations, with a hosted tier); Zep/Graphiti (temporal knowledge-graph memory); Letta (productionized MemGPT). For Claude Code specifically, the native mechanism is `CLAUDE.md` project memory plus hooks — a correction written into `CLAUDE.md` is re-injected into every session. `unverified: current release/maturity status of Mem0, Zep, Letta, and LangMem` — these move quickly and should be checked against their repos at write-up time.

**Enforcement vs. storage.** Most of these systems *store and retrieve* rules (Mem0, Zep, MemGPT/Letta, Generative Agents) and rely on the model to honor them at generation time — retrieval is a soft prompt-level nudge, not a hard gate. The systems that actually *enforce* compile a rule into a checkable artifact: Constitutional AI's critique-revision pass, Voyager's executable skill code, and — in the CLI-agent world — hooks and eval suites that run deterministically outside the model. That distinction (soft retrieval vs. hard gate) is the axis nexus should rank on.

**Relevance to nexus.** None of the Evidence block bears on this sub-question — the gnosis hits are all nexus build transcripts about ratchet tests (`tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py:159`, `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py:118`) and CLI wiring (`nexus_cli/cli.py`), and the atlas hits are nexus source symbols (`nexus_cli/atlas.py:131`, `nexus_cli/benchmark.py:39`). The academic/tooling claims above stand on general knowledge plus the web sources cited, not on repository evidence.

## 2. Libraries, memory layers, and guardrail frameworks for CLI agents

**Memory layers / self-editing agents**

- **Letta (formerly MemGPT)** — agent server/runtime where the agent manages its own memory blocks (core, archival, recall) via tool calls; memory persists across sessions. Exposes REST API and MCP server, so a CLI agent talks to it over HTTP or MCP. Maturity: production-oriented, active. Cost: OSS (Apache-2.0), self-hostable; hosted option paid. Enforcement: memory is *stored and re-injected* into the system prompt each turn — enforces by prompt construction, not by blocking output.
- **LangMem** (LangChain) — SDK for extracting and updating long-term memory (semantic, episodic, procedural) from conversation, with a prompt-optimizer that rewrites the system prompt from feedback. Maturity: beta/early, tied to LangGraph. Cost: OSS (MIT). Enforcement: procedural memory injected into prompt; no output-side gate.
- **Mem0 / Zep** — managed memory layers with add/search APIs and graph or temporal stores. Maturity: Mem0 widely used OSS + hosted; Zep is a temporal knowledge-graph service. Cost: OSS core, paid cloud. Enforcement: retrieval-augmented prompt injection only.

**Guardrail frameworks (output-side enforcement)**

- **NeMo Guardrails** (NVIDIA) — runtime between app and LLM, with Colang-defined dialogue flows, input/output rails, and dialog rails that can force a response or refuse. Maturity: production, actively maintained. Cost: OSS (Apache-2.0). Enforcement: *intercepts and can rewrite/block* model output — the strongest "enforce, not just store" option in the list.
- **Guardrails AI** — validators (Pydantic-style) applied to LLM output with re-asking on failure; hub of prebuilt validators. Maturity: production OSS (Apache-2.0) + hosted. Enforcement: output validation with retry/reask loops.
- **Llama Guard / prompt-guard classifiers** — safety classifiers runnable as pre/post filter. Enforcement: classification gate, not rule-learning.

Web sources corroborate the guardrail category: GuardAgent and DSLs like Guardrail provide runtime enforcement by intercepting agent actions against user-defined constraints [7](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGeQEki8A9T6VtyDrF6-bvXAuhLlNn9iuFojzjm7KC0rRitwHiRVzflpxWRIZZnVWCzWoef_GqAjV8HWjQmv5D-PpBJUYn7pU1wovtcEqst7qDhiwRdYqbOEg==), and enforcement mechanisms are commonly categorized into three layers: prompt-based (e.g., `.cursorrules`, `SOUL.md`), tool-based (hooks/CI linting), and architecture-based (hardcoded policy engines) [8](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGOfpszA9eSoYM1tm-QlDPgkG2ULlLexe3tmyaNV4-jBiRuPkSeUejvJEXsSgsdirCKgncveq4FQf0GGYhrI-1AQBRnKu3d5a1ByGRhDfDD4Ds8aNPpSR8mwZCQY7-1yk5Tv1x3FQJ_ILTt2ZLqK6U=).

**How these reach a CLI agent (Claude Code / opencode).** Claude Code supports hooks (e.g. `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`) configured in settings JSON, plus `CLAUDE.md` / system-prompt injection and MCP servers. opencode similarly supports plugins/hooks and MCP. Integration patterns: (a) a `UserPromptSubmit`/`Stop` hook that calls a guardrail service and can block or rewrite; (b) an MCP server exposing a memory layer (Letta, Mem0) as tools; (c) `CLAUDE.md`/system-prompt injection for stored rules. The hook path is what gives *enforcement* — a `Stop`/`PreToolUse` hook can veto, whereas prompt injection only nudges. `unverified: Claude Code hook event names (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit/Stop) and opencode plugin API` — I did not read a repo doc or code file confirming them.

**Fleet-wide propagation caveat.** None of these libraries natively fan a correction out to every agent in a fleet; they are per-agent or per-service. Reaching "every agent" requires a shared store (a memory service or a rules file) plus each CLI agent configured to read it — the propagation layer is yours to build.

**Ranked shortlist for nexus**

1. **NeMo Guardrails** — only option that enforces on the output path (block/rewrite), OSS, hookable.
2. **Letta** — best durable, self-editing memory with an MCP/HTTP surface a CLI agent can consume.

## 4. Architectures for propagating corrections/rules across a multi-agent fleet

**1. Git-backed instruction files (the "shared file as source of truth" pattern).** The dominant pattern in this fleet is a single canonical instruction file in a git repo that every agent reads at session start. The nexus repo itself is the shared store: agents resolve the real wrapper to `~/nexus/nexus_cli/cli.py` and pull the same copy (gnosis `transcript:.treehouse:e7827ad7-2a2f-4bfc-af2d-d73a8e0d6102:241`), and the Windows handoff doc documents an injection bundle composed from the repo (gnosis `doc:nexus:docs/nexus-windows-session-handoff-2026-07-10.md#004`, `python -m nexus_cli.cli atlas-inject compose --project nexus --repo D:\d...`). Propagation is by `git pull`; enforcement is by the agent reading the file. Lowest-cost, highest-maturity option and already the fleet's de facto mechanism.

**2. Centralized index / registry with a reconcile step.** `nexus_cli/atlas.py` exposes `reconcile` (atlas `D:\Dev\nexus\nexus_cli\atlas.py:131`) and `walk` (`atlas.py:235`) — a walk-then-reconcile shape that scans a source tree and syncs a central index. That is the architecture for "corrections land in one store, then a reconcile pass fans them out to every consumer." `nexus_cli/benchmark.py:39` (`compare`) is the analogous scoring hook for evaluating replies against a rubric.

**3. Ratchet tests as the enforcement layer (not just storage).** Rules are encoded as pytest ratchets that fail the build when violated: `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py` (atlas `D:\Dev\nexus\tests\test_orphan_ratchet.py:118-159`, class `TestTheDetectorIsGenerousOnPurpose`), plus `test_function_orphan_ratchet.py` and `test_no_raw_subprocess_spawns.py` (gnosis `transcript:.treehouse:8a80c466-b5b7-435c-af62-93c5f9853298:117`, `transcript:.treehouse:02b23c7a-a153-4c48-ab04-31691556de98:113`). A correction becomes durable by being distilled into a ratchet test that runs on every push — enforced at merge time, not merely stored. The project rules confirm this: `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py` fails if a new `nexus_cli/` module isn't wired in.

**4. Pub/sub and shared vector/relational stores.** No evidence in the provided hits of a pub/sub sync layer or a shared vector store in this fleet. `unverified: a pub/sub or vector-store propagation mechanism exists in nexus` — the evidence shows git + reconcile + ratchet tests, not a message bus.

## 5. Ranked shortlist for nexus

**1. Ratchet tests as the enforcement mechanism (highest fit, lowest cost).** The nexus repo already has a working pattern for "learn a rule once, then make it impossible to regress": the orphan ratchet. `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py` exists and is structured around a deliberately generous detector (`TestTheDetectorIsGenerousOnPurpose`, `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py:118-159`), and prior runs show the same shape being applied to functions (`test_function_orphan_ratchet.py`) and to subprocess spawning (`test_no_raw_subprocess_spawns.py`) — gnosis `transcript:.treehouse:8a80c466-b5b7-435c-af62-93c5f9853298:117` and `transcript:.treehouse:02b23c7a-a153-4c48-ab04-31691556de98:113`. This is *enforcement*, not storage: a correction ("don't do X") becomes a test that fails the pre-push gate, so the rule is re-checked on every future change rather than remembered. Complexity is low (a new `tests/test_*.py`), operational cost is zero beyond existing pytest, and it is pure Python 3.10-compatible. Caveat: the ratchet must not use `os.chmod`-based unwritability, POSIX-only calls, or a bare `import tomllib` — the project rules record two swarm merges already blocked by exactly those (run `pilot-f12fd160aa7e-1788690199`).

**2. A memory/guideline layer surfaced through the existing CLI injection path (medium fit, medium cost).** nexus already has an injection mechanism: `python -m nexus_cli.cli atlas-inject compose --project nexus --repo ...` is documented as producing a full injection bundle with all sections and "why" grounded (gnosis `doc:nexus:docs/nexus-windows-session-handoff-2026-07-10.md#004`). A durable communication-rule store that feeds this compose step would reach every agent that runs the injection, which is the fleet-wide requirement. Cost is the wiring: per project rules a new `nexus_cli/` module must be referenced by name from an existing `.py` module, `deploy/`, `scripts/`, or carry a `__main__` block, or `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py` fails — so the store and its wiring must land in the same task. New subcommands register in `nexus_cli/cli.py` (gnosis `transcript:.treehouse:e7827ad7-2a2f-4bfc-af2d-d73a8e0d6102:241` confirms the real wrapper resolves to `~/nexus/nexus_cli/cli.py`). This is storage-plus-delivery; it does not by itself enforce, so it should be paired with #1.

**3. A guard/placement check in the existing guard logic (medium fit, low cost).** nexus already has guard logic in `nexus_cli/placement.py` (gnosis `transcript:.treehouse:fdd728bb-8676-4d43-8f33-338b724e0061:31`), the natural place to add a runtime refusal for a corrected behavior. Lower rank than #1 because a runtime guard only fires on the code path it guards, whereas a ratchet test covers the whole repo.

**4. External self-learning frameworks (lowest fit for this fleet).** General reflection-loop / preference-learning systems are the literature answer to the original question, but none of the evidence here ties any specific framework to nexus's CLI, its injection path, or its Windows/3.10 gate. `unverified: any specific external framework's Python 3.10 compatibility, cost, or ability to reach every agent in this fleet` — no file:line or gnosis node in the evidence supports a named tool, so none is ranked above the in-repo mechanisms that are demonstrably wired.

**Ranking rationale.** Order is driven by four criteria: #1 wins on complexity (one test file), cost (zero), 3.10 compatibility (plain pytest), and effectiveness (it *blocks* the merge, which is enforcement). #2 wins on reach (every agent that composes the injection bundle) but only stores/delivers. #3 is cheap but narrow. #4 is unverified for this codebase.

**Unknown:** whether nexus already has a dedicated communication-rule store or a `nexus_cli/` module for it — the evidence shows injection (`atlas-inject compose`) and guard logic (`nexus_cli/placement.py`) but no memory-layer module; a search of `nexus_cli/` for such a module would settle whether #2 is new work or an extension.

## 6. Cost-benefit analysis

The original question's cost dimension, addressed explicitly:

**Token/latency cost of reflection loops.** Reflection loops significantly increase token usage and latency due to iterative generation — the "cost-per-improvement" metric [2](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEFuOrhsjVmN3jDIXmCx10KzfTrZjTyzKNRjeuLIqnXgFYriPvLn7naqgmev_UznJfPXYm7n8rWUJdpiNsLplNNtQWSgl-ISWI3062LslYt9p4E6ljrMOxCxwPpqEsFjVkWOE57gyM=) [11](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGXn6-1TuU8rginTg64ePzD14smi_XyKXS1MxMJQSSwAhGJW_yfoJ1YU-s5UNcRXQflWhrBDFVyCimxOrlQ3Dlu5_72kYG3SepGsDRQEza2XgQZWWWd9rIANMcYXJMTmixgmFxxr69jK-TBffkmfFlm8_PVIjhey9J4uGM=). Distillation into smaller models (e.g., sLMs) is the primary strategy for reducing inference costs while maintaining high-quality, task-specific behavioral rules [12](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkZE4SgHE5djDJ42Dyg5ilGDb-PFpGA_IHuqhGlHtxKJxyI0A8h6H8Wm9Z34vas-7T2dtacwf6ixKo64aWzc94cqntjWPQSFjyujbUi6plWxp9079wbA==) [13](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHLFVeBvEtdi5X1gYHAvv76iqKtfXx0bB_5eA9umx6vJdWYfvmO4N8tWS3mbRBjwMPFca4dRVKaaWWebfaudzBE6YpT_UAShe6R20WhzD3uCQRRVqXayG4tBb8mNzV93r_498FOPNRgB_v4A7OLzw==).

**Cost of the ranked options for nexus.**

- **Ratchet tests (#1):** zero marginal cost. They run inside the existing pytest suite on the existing pre-push gate; no new service, no API calls, no storage. The only cost is authoring time for the test file. This is the best cost/benefit ratio in the shortlist.
- **Memory/guideline layer via `atlas-inject compose` (#2):** low-to-moderate. If the store is a git-backed file (the fleet's existing pattern), cost is essentially the wiring work plus the compose-step integration. If it becomes a hosted memory service (Mem0/Zep cloud), cost shifts to per-request API calls and vector-store hosting — the web sources note that local-only file-based implementations are essentially zero-cost while cloud-hosted vectors add external API costs [6](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGrvpDX8tjXLby5vKigyOcd8MQbUaXGwMaRoAJkZKtQKWm4zgiUMKRsm7PCyM6EEFa9Mlg7CkV5QrmG0KN8409kU-LDY3JVV7_gDlpcbT3hEnJNhBI5X8GVGqf1FP0p-WSy9m9TygYAK5ZjwF4-szqiBmYl8tpP4jj-sYlVuB63w4J-DhuKbn0UhWRYdBMjjQUNQQ==) [3](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFrYEfyv91MWem4DEQc_k43tZwXI3RwY527upbWv1QBAi0

ready.title: nexus: research proven model-routing methods for the model picker
ready.body:
Captain 2026-10-05 17:31Z: "Do research as well to see if there's any sort of methods to build into this tool, something that's very successful, widely admired, or used, or maybe find something that's new and cutting edges even better if there's something that exists... this model picker needs to have a robust ability from like a one-liner to like deep info on the task and the job at hand for the data that's being managed by the job."

Research question: what proven and cutting-edge methods exist for choosing the right LLM per job by ability and cost? Cover learned routers (RouteLLM, Not Diamond, Martian, OpenRouter auto routing, Arch-Router), cascades (FrugalGPT), benchmark-driven selection (RouterBench), LLM-as-judge outcome scoring, and bandit or online learning from logged outcomes. For each: how it decides, what data it needs, published savings and quality, open-source availability and licence, and whether it accepts anything from a one-line task description to a full task spec. Recommend what to adopt or copy for a self-hosted picker fed by our own per-job logs (cost, tokens, success, rework).

# Research Report

**Question:** nexus: research proven model-routing methods for the model picker

Captain 2026-10-05 17:31Z: "Do research as well to see if there's any sort of methods to build into this tool, something that's very successful, widely admired, or used, or maybe find something that's new and cutting edges even better if there's something that exists... this model picker needs to have a robust ability from like a one-liner to like deep info on the task and the job at hand for the data that's being managed by the job."

Research question: what proven and cutting-edge methods exist for choosing the right LLM per job by ability and cost? Cover learned routers (RouteLLM, Not Diamond, Martian, OpenRouter auto routing, Arch-Router), cascades (FrugalGPT), benchmark-driven selection (RouterBench), LLM-as-judge outcome scoring, and bandit or online learning from logged outcomes. For each: how it decides, what data it needs, published savings and quality, open-source availability and licence, and whether it accepts anything from a one-line task description to a full task spec. Recommend what to adopt or copy for a self-hosted picker fed by our own per-job logs (cost, tokens, success, rework).

## Sub‑questions
1. What are the decision mechanisms, input requirements (one-line prompt vs. deep task spec), published cost/quality trade-offs, and open-source licenses of learned routing systems such as RouteLLM, Arch-Router, Not Diamond, Martian, and OpenRouter auto-routing?
2. How do cascade-based routing strategies like FrugalGPT and evaluation frameworks like RouterBench make routing decisions, what cost savings and accuracy retention do they demonstrate, and are their reference implementations open-source?
3. What contextual bandit and online learning algorithms (e.g., LinUCB, contextual Thompson sampling) are established for dynamic LLM routing, and how do they formalize multi-objective reward functions incorporating cost, token count, task success, and rework?
4. What architectures and best practices exist for LLM-as-judge outcome scoring to evaluate and label per-job completion quality and rework likelihood from historical interaction logs?
5. What concrete system architecture and algorithmic design should be adopted for a self-hosted, Python 3.10-compatible model picker that scores candidates using local embeddings and historical telemetry (cost, tokens, success, rework) across both brief one-liners and detailed task specs?

## Draft
# Model Picker for nexus: Decision Mechanisms, Evaluation, and a Self-Hosted Architecture

## 1. Learned routers: decision mechanisms, inputs, trade-offs, licences

**RouteLLM (LMSYS).** A learned binary router: it trains a preference/win-prediction model on Chatbot Arena battle data to estimate P(strong model wins | query), then routes to the strong model only when that probability exceeds a cost threshold calibrated to a target fraction of strong-model calls. Input is the raw prompt text (a single user turn is enough; no structured task spec required). Published result: ~95% of GPT-4 quality at ~85% cost reduction on MT-Bench-style evaluations, with the threshold tunable along the cost/quality curve. Open-source, Apache-2.0, with pretrained router checkpoints released. *(These are the project's own published figures; no repo file:line or gnosis node in the findings states them — treat the specific percentages and the licence string as `unverified` against this codebase.)*

**Arch-Router (Katanemo).** A small fine-tuned model that maps a query to one of a user-declared set of named "domains"/routes (e.g. `code`, `legal`, `chat`) rather than to a specific model; the operator then binds each route to a model. Decision input is the prompt plus the route definitions; it works from a one-liner but benefits from a richer description of the task. It is a 1.5B-class model, so it is cheap to self-host. Open-source under Apache-2.0. *(No repo file:line; the licence and size are `unverified` against this codebase.)*

**Not Diamond.** A hosted meta-model router: you send the prompt (and optionally a task description, quality/latency/cost preference, and candidate model list) and it returns a chosen model. It learns from its own evaluation corpus plus your feedback, so it needs an API key and outbound calls — it is not self-hostable. Pricing is per-routing-call; the model itself is closed. *(Closed-source and hosted — `unverified` against this codebase.)*

**Martian.** Similar hosted router/meta-model with a "model mapping" product; closed-source, API-based, decides from the prompt plus configured preferences. *(Closed-source — `unverified` against this codebase.)*

**OpenRouter auto-routing.** Not a learned router in the RouteLLM sense: OpenRouter exposes a `models` array with fallback ordering and a `:nitro`/`:floor` style suffix, and its "auto" behaviour is largely price/availability-based selection plus provider fallback rather than a trained quality predictor. Input is the normal chat request; no task spec needed. The service is proprietary, but the client is just an OpenAI-compatible HTTP call. This codebase already talks to OpenRouter: `tests/test_models_openrouter.py:54` (`test_openrouter_gateway_maps_to_openrouter_tier`) and the `openrouter:{OPENROUTER_MODEL}` model-id construction at `tests/test_models_openrouter.py:0` show the gateway→tier mapping and the `openrouter:` prefix convention; `tests/test_proxy_openrouter.py:95` (`openrouter_key`) shows the key fixture. ## 2. Cascade routing (FrugalGPT) and evaluation frameworks (RouterBench)

**FrugalGPT — how it decides.** FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia, Zou, arXiv 2305.05176) is a *cascade*: a query is sent to a cheap model first; a learned **scorer** estimates whether that answer is good enough, and only if it fails does the query escalate to the next, more expensive model in the chain. The scorer is trained on a small set of labeled query/answer pairs to predict answer quality, so the cascade's decision rule is "accept if predicted quality ≥ threshold, else escalate." The key data requirement is a modest labeled calibration set (the paper reports training the scorer on a few thousand examples) plus per-model cost/latency figures; it does **not** need a full task spec — a query string is enough, since the scorer operates on the query and the candidate answer.

**FrugalGPT — published results.** The paper reports cost reductions of up to ~98% versus always calling GPT-4 at comparable or better accuracy on its benchmark suite, with the headline configuration matching GPT-4's accuracy at roughly 1/10th to 1/100th of the cost depending on the task. These are the paper's own numbers on its own benchmarks, not independently reproduced figures. *(No `kind: web` source URL for these figures appears in the findings — treat the ~98% figure as `unsupported`.)*

**RouterBench — how it decides.** RouterBench (arXiv 2403.12031) is not a router itself but an **evaluation harness**: it provides a dataset of ~405k inference outcomes across 11 LLMs on a shared prompt set, with per-response quality scores and costs, so that routing methods can be compared on a common footing. It defines the routing problem as picking a model per query to maximize quality subject to a cost budget, and it evaluates both "cascades" and "predictive routers" (a router that predicts each model's quality for a query and picks the best under budget). Its data requirement is exactly the kind of artifact nexus would need to build: a matrix of (query, model) → quality and cost. *(No `kind: web` source URL for the ~405k figure appears in the findings — treat it as `unsupported`.)*

**RouterBench — published results.** The paper's central finding is that a well-trained predictive router can capture most of the quality of the best single model at a fraction of the cost, and that simple cost-aware routing beats always-using-the-best-model on the cost/quality frontier. It also shows that routing gains are task-dependent and that a router trained on one distribution degrades out of distribution — a caution for a self-hosted picker fed only its own logs. *(No `kind: web` source URL for these findings appears in the findings — treat as `unsupported`.)*

**Open-source availability.** Both have reference implementations on GitHub: FrugalGPT's cascade code is published by the authors (Stanford HazyResearch lineage), and RouterBench's dataset and evaluation code are released under permissive licences (MIT/Apache-style) — but those repos were not read in this session, so the exact licence text is `unverified: the precise licence file and terms of the FrugalGPT and RouterBench reference repositories`. The general pattern (cascade + scorer, and a logged-outcome matrix for evaluation) is well-established and reproducible without their code.

**Fit for nexus.** The cascade pattern maps directly onto nexus's per-job logs: the logs already carry cost, tokens, success, and rework (per the Context block), which is exactly the (query, model) → quality/cost matrix RouterBench assumes. A FrugalGPT-style cascade needs only a small labeled calibration set on top of those logs, and accepts anything from a one-line task description (the query string) upward — it does not require a full task spec. The RouterBench lesson to copy is the evaluation harness: build the outcome matrix first, then compare a cheap-first cascade against a predictive router on it.

## 3. Contextual bandits and online learning for dynamic LLM routing

**The core formalization.** Dynamic LLM routing is naturally a *contextual bandit* problem: at each round you observe a context (the task/job), choose one of K arms (models), and receive a reward (quality minus cost). You never observe the counterfactual — what a different model would have produced — which is exactly the bandit setting. The two canonical algorithm families are:

- **LinUCB** (Li et al., 2010, "A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation"): assumes the expected reward is linear in a feature vector of context × arm, `E[r | x, a] = xᵀθ_a`, maintains a ridge-regression estimate `θ_a` per arm with covariance `A_a`, and picks `argmax_a (xᵀθ_a + α·√(xᵀA_a⁻¹x))`. The bonus term is an explicit exploration knob; α trades exploration against exploitation. It needs a *feature vector* per (context, arm) — for LLM routing that means embedding the task description plus per-model features (price, context window, historical success). *(No `kind: web` source URL for the Li et al. 2010 citation appears in the findings — treat the citation as `unsupported`.)*
- **Contextual Thompson sampling** (Agrawal & Goyal, 2013, "Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits with Linear Payoffs"): same linear model, but instead of a deterministic UCB bonus it samples `θ̃_a` from the posterior `N(θ_a, A_a⁻¹)` and picks the arm with the highest sampled reward. It typically explores more gracefully and is the standard choice when you want probabilistic arm selection. *(No `kind: web` source URL for the Agrawal & Goyal 2013 citation appears in the findings — treat the citation as `unsupported`.)*

Both are *online*: they update after every logged outcome, so they learn from your own traffic rather than a static benchmark. This is the key property for a self-hosted picker fed by per-job logs.

**Multi-objective reward.** The standard trick is scalarization: define `r = quality − λ·cost` (or a weighted sum `w_q·quality − w_c·cost − w_t·tokens − w_r·rework`), then run a single-objective bandit on `r`. Cost and token count are directly observable from the API response (usage fields), so they enter the reward as negative terms; task success and rework are the quality signal. The weakness of scalarization is that it collapses the Pareto frontier into one λ — you must pick the exchange rate between quality and dollars up front. Alternatives are (a) **constrained bandits / bandits with knapsacks**, where cost is a budget constraint rather than a reward term, and (b) **multi-objective bandits** that maintain a Pareto front of arms and let a policy pick from it. For a picker that must respect a spend cap, the constrained formulation is usually the better fit.

**How the reward signals map to your logs.** Cost and token count come straight from the provider usage payload. Task success and rework are the hard part and are typically supplied by an **LLM-as-judge** or a downstream signal (did the test pass, did the human re-ask, was the diff reverted). The bandit only needs a scalar per logged round; the judge is what produces it. This is why the bandit layer and the judge layer are usually designed together.

**Cold start.** Bandits need data before they beat a heuristic. The standard pattern is to warm-start with a benchmark- or heuristic-based policy (e.g., route by task class) and let the bandit take over as logs accumulate, or to use a *hybrid*: a learned router for the arms you have data on, a fallback rule for the rest.

**What is and is not verifiable from the findings.** The findings contain no code or document describing a bandit implementation in nexus — the hits are about cost routing policy, OpenRouter plumbing, and ratchet tests, not LinUCB/Thompson code. Specifically:

- `gnosis: memory:-home-justin-gnosis:feedback_cost_routing` documents a *rule-based* cost-routing policy ("route tasks by cost. Claude inline for reasoning/integration, `roundtable code` for code generation, LMStudio…") — this is a static heuristic, not a learned bandit.
- `gnosis: transcript:nexus-brain:62bc431d-a0b9-4f73-8d76-5f57779904c6:400` records a routing-rule failure ("Our routing rules still send investigations and design work to Claude Opus") — evidence that the current nexus routing is rule-based and has cost-leak problems, which is precisely the motivation for a learned router.
- `gnosis: doc:nexus-cand:docs/atlas-digest-budget-spec-2026-07-10.md#006` describes a *byte-budget cascade with truncation logging* — a budget mechanism, not a bandit.

So: **unverified: any existing LinUCB / Thompson-sampling implementation inside nexus** — no file:line or gnosis node in the findings shows one. The algorithms above are established published methods (Li et al. 2010; Agrawal & Goyal 2013), not claims about nexus code.

**Recommendation for the picker.** For a self-hosted picker fed by per-job logs (cost, tokens, success, rework), the pragmatic design is: (1) log every job as `(context_features, chosen_model, cost, tokens, success, rework)`; (2) scalarize to `r = success − w_c·cost − w_t·tokens − w_r·rework` with weights you can tune; (3) run **LinUCB** first because it is simple, deterministic, and easy to debug, with **contextual Thompson sampling** as the upgrade if you want smoother exploration; (4) warm-start from the existing rule-based policy (`feedback_cost_routing`) so the picker is never worse than the heuristic during cold start; (5) keep the reward weights and the judge that produces `success`/`rework` as separate, auditable components, since the bandit is only as good as its reward signal.

## 4. LLM-as-judge outcome scoring: architectures and best practices

**1. Pointwise vs. pairwise vs. listwise judging.** The three canonical architectures are: (a) *pointwise* — one model scores a single response against a rubric or reference (absolute score, often 1–5 or 0–1); (b) *pairwise* — the judge sees two candidate outputs and picks a winner (or tie), which is the format used by Chatbot Arena-style Elo/Bradley-Terry ranking and by MT-Bench; (c) *listwise* — the judge ranks N candidates at once. Pairwise is generally the most reliable because it removes the judge's need to calibrate an absolute scale, but it costs O(N²) comparisons to rank N candidates. For a per-job picker fed by historical logs, pointwise scoring is the practical choice because each logged job already has exactly one outcome to label — there is no second candidate to compare against.

**2. Reference-based vs. reference-free.** Reference-based judging compares the output to a gold answer or rubric; reference-free judging scores against the task description alone. Reference-free is what you need for a self-hosted picker, because most logged jobs will not have a gold answer. The judge prompt then becomes: given the task spec (one-liner to full spec) and the logged output, score completion quality and estimate rework likelihood.

**3. Rubric decomposition and chain-of-thought.** Best practice is to have the judge emit structured sub-scores (e.g. correctness, completeness, instruction-following, format) plus a short rationale before the final score, rather than a single holistic number. Decomposed rubrics reduce variance and make the label auditable. This is the "G-Eval"-style pattern (chain-of-thought + form-filling) and is the dominant open pattern.

**4. Bias controls.** Documented judge biases that must be mitigated: *position bias* (pairwise judges favor the first or second slot — mitigate by swapping order and averaging), *verbosity bias* (longer answers score higher — mitigate by length-normalizing or explicitly instructing against it), *self-preference bias* (a model favors its own outputs — mitigate by using a judge from a different family than the candidates), and *score clustering* (judges over-use the middle of the scale — mitigate with few-shot anchors at each scale point). These are well-established findings from the MT-Bench / LLM-as-a-judge literature.

**5. Agreement with human labels.** The standard validation step is to measure judge–human agreement (Cohen's kappa or Spearman correlation) on a held-out sample of human-labeled jobs, and to report it alongside the judge's scores. A judge that does not clear a threshold (commonly ~0.7–0.8 agreement) should not be trusted to auto-label training data for the router.

**6. Using judge labels for the router.** The judge output is a *label*, not a routing decision. The pipeline is: logged job (task text, model used, cost, tokens, success flag, rework flag) → judge scores completion quality and rework likelihood → labels become the target variable for a learned router or bandit. This is exactly the "LLM-as-judge outcome scoring" leg of the original question, and it is what makes a self-hosted picker trainable from your own logs rather than from a public benchmark.

**7. Cost/latency of judging.** Judging every logged job with a frontier model is expensive; the standard mitigation is to judge a sampled subset, or to use a cheaper judge model and periodically re-validate it against the expensive one. This matters for nexus because the picker's whole purpose is cost control.

**8. Rework likelihood specifically.** Rework is a *downstream* signal (the job was re-run, edited, or reverted), so it is best modeled as a separate binary/ordinal label rather than folded into a quality score. If the logs carry a rework flag, that flag is a stronger and cheaper label than a judge score; the judge is most valuable for the jobs where no rework flag exists or where you want a quality gradient rather than a binary.

## 5. Architecture for a self-hosted, Python 3.10-compatible model picker

**Core design: a two-stage retrieve-then-score picker with a telemetry-fed cost/quality model.**

### 5.1 Candidate retrieval (cheap, deterministic)
Maintain a static registry of candidate models with per-model metadata: provider, context window, price per input/output token, capability tags. This mirrors the existing pattern in the fleet — `roundtable/knowledge/providers.md#openrouter` (atlas: `/home/justin/roundtable/roundtable/knowledge/providers.md:113`) is a documented provider registry, and the hive test suite already models an OpenRouter tier mapping (`projects/hive/tests/test_models_openrouter.py:54`, `test_openrouter_gateway_maps_to_openrouter_tier`). Retrieval filters that registry by hard constraints (context length, required capability, provider availability) before any scoring — this keeps the expensive scoring step small.

### 5.2 Feature extraction from the task (handles one-liner → full spec)
The picker must accept anything from a one-line description to a full task spec. The robust approach is to embed the task text with a **local embedding model** (no network dependency, works on 3.10) and derive a small feature vector:
- embedding of the task text (semantic difficulty/domain signal),
- cheap surface features: token count of the prompt, presence of code blocks, number of files/artifacts referenced, explicit "reasoning"/"design" keywords.

This is the same "route by task shape" idea already recorded in the fleet's cost-routing memory: `memory:-home-justin-gnosis:feedback_cost_routing` — *"route tasks by cost. Claude inline for reasoning/integration, `roundtable code` for code generation, LMStudio…"*. That memory is a hand-written rule table; the picker generalizes it into a learned scorer.

### 5.3 Scoring model (learned from local telemetry)
Train a lightweight regressor/classifier (logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees — both pure-Python/sklearn, 3.10-safe) that predicts, per (task-features, candidate-model) pair:
- **expected success probability** (from historical success/rework labels),
- **expected cost** = predicted tokens × per-model price.

Then rank by a utility function, e.g. `utility = P(success) − λ · expected_cost`, with λ tunable per job class. This is the "bandit / online learning from logged outcomes" family: the model is retrained on the per-job logs (cost, tokens, success, rework) the operator already collects. Cold-start for a new model uses its published benchmark scores as a prior, then blends toward observed telemetry as data accumulates.

### 5.4 Telemetry schema
Each logged job should record: task text (or its embedding), chosen model, input/output tokens, computed cost, success flag, rework flag/count. This is exactly the data the picker needs and is consistent with the fleet's existing usage-capture work — the treehouse transcript describes probing "raw OpenRouter responses at a tiny max_tokens, plus what the stable (live) and worktree `_extract_usage` store" (`transcript:.treehouse:0ba19423-c6cc-4721-a4d5-f1efbc4a8909:35`), i.e. a `_extract_usage` path already exists to harvest token/cost data.

# Research Report

**Question:** nexus: research model and harness capability data for the model picker

Captain 2026-10-05 18:16Z: "the research should cover this part ... see what people are doing? Are we doing something really good? Are there better ways to do it? Are there more efficient ways to do it? What about data sets that help us determine or details or information about models and harnesses and also like Some harnesses might need tools. So what harnesses have what tools or plugins or mods and what is needed for each job, too, right? So this all has to be part of the research as well."

Research questions: (1) How do teams running many coding and agent jobs today choose model and harness per job (agent harnesses such as Claude Code, opencode, Codex, Aider, OpenHands, Cline; orchestrator-plus-cheap-worker fan-out; direct single calls versus agent loops), and what measured results do they publish? (2) Which public datasets and catalogs give machine-readable model capabilities and prices (models.dev, OpenRouter models API, LiteLLM model cost map, Artificial Analysis, LMArena, Aider polyglot leaderboard, SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench), what fields each has (context window, output limit, tool calling, reasoning, price, speed), licence, and how fresh they are? (3) Which datasets or benchmarks compare harnesses (not just models), and what tools, plugins, MCP servers or mods each major harness needs for coding, research, review and one-shot jobs? (4) When is a direct API call better than an agent harness, with evidence on context overhead and cost? (5) What would make our setup (a firstmate supervisor, Sonnet leads fanning out free-model calls, a LangGraph hive with free and DeepSeek profiles, Jev as a fast classifier) better or more efficient by those standards?

## Sub‑questions
1. What published benchmarks, routing architectures, and empirical results exist from teams dynamically selecting models and agent harnesses (e.g. Claude Code, Aider, OpenHands, Cline) for coding and agent workloads?
2. What machine-readable schemas, update frequencies, access methods, and license terms do public model catalogs (such as OpenRouter API, LiteLLM cost map, Artificial Analysis, models.dev, and SWE-bench/Terminal-Bench) provide for context window, tool calling, reasoning, pricing, and latency?
3. Which benchmarks specifically evaluate agent harnesses (rather than standalone models), and what tools, plugins, or MCP servers does each major harness require for coding, research, review, and one-shot jobs?
4. What empirical data exists comparing direct single API calls against iterative agent harness loops regarding context window inflation, token cost overhead, latency, and task completion rates?
5. Based on current industry routing and fan-out patterns, what concrete architecture or configuration changes would improve the efficiency and success rates of nexus's setup (firstmate supervisor, Sonnet leads fanning out free models, LangGraph profiles, and Jev classifier)?

## Draft
# Published benchmarks, routing architectures, and empirical results for dynamic model/harness selection

## 1. Benchmarks that compare harnesses, not just models

The public comparators usually named here are the Aider polyglot leaderboard, SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified, and Terminal-Bench. The evidence I can actually ground is thinner than the question implies: **no published cross-harness benchmark table (Claude Code vs Aider vs OpenHands vs Cline on identical tasks) appears anywhere in the findings**, and no leaderboard numbers for Aider polyglot / SWE-bench / Terminal-Bench are cited either. Both remain **unknown** — settling them would require retrieving the leaderboards directly.

The one harness-vs-harness empirical result in the evidence is internal, not published: the hive swarm's own reviewer comparison, where "DeepSeek now catches 15 of 19 and sends back 5 of 16 good diffs, against 6 of 16 on main. The all-model false-fix rate falls from 24 to 21 of 96" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:684), with an intermediate state of "18 of 19 defects (was 5), but it wrongly sends 8 of 16 good diffs back for fixes (was 2)" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:441). That is a real measured harness/model-swap result — swapping the reviewer model changed both defect-catch and false-reject rates, and the tradeoff was rounds/cost, not raw accuracy. It is a single internal run, not a published leaderboard.

The gnosis landscape doc that does compare tooling is about memory/code-graph tools, not agent harnesses — "Memory + Code-Graph Landscape — What to Steal for gnosis+atlas (2026-06-21)" (gnosis doc:gnosis:docs/archive/memory-codegraph-landscape-2026-06-21.md#001), with a cost/tool-call claim "~16% cheaper / ~58% fewer tool calls (colbymchenry/codegraph)" sourced from a GitHub README benchmark table (gnosis doc:gnosis:docs/archive/memory-codegraph-landscape-2026-06-21.md#008) — that is a code-graph tool, not a harness.

**Unknown:** a published, cross-harness benchmark (Claude Code / Aider / OpenHands / Cline on identical tasks) with measured pass rates — no such result appears in the findings, and it would settle the "which harness" half of the sub-question. **Unknown:** the exact Aider polyglot / SWE-bench / Terminal-Bench leaderboard numbers and their freshness — none are cited in the findings, and I did not retrieve them.

## 2. Machine-readable model catalogs: schemas, freshness, access, licensing

**OpenRouter models API.** OpenRouter exposes a public model list over HTTP; the fleet already consumes it. `atlas: /home/justin/gnosis/tests/test_proxy_openrouter.py:95` (`openrouter_key`) and `atlas: /home/justin/vpsmate-home/projects/hive/tests/test_models_openrouter.py:54` (`test_openrouter_gateway_maps_to_openrouter_tier`) show the gateway mapping an `openrouter:<model>` id to an OpenRouter tier, and `atlas: /home/justin/hive/tests/test_models_openrouter.py:0` shows the `f'openrouter:{OPENROUTER_MODEL}'` id form. The catalog is queried live (no bundled snapshot): `gnosis: transcript:nexus-brain:ab376a73-3982-4c38-9da6-9113cc35ab03:174` records that "OpenRouter's public model list has no Jev, typesafe or System One model" — i.e. the list is the authoritative live source and was checked directly. `gnosis: transcript:nexus-brain:62bc431d-a0b9-4f73-8d76-5f57779904c6:70` shows a real call plus account-balance check against the same API. Fields: OpenRouter's `/api/v1/models` returns per-model `id`, `context_length`, `pricing` (prompt/completion per token), `supported_parameters` (which includes `tools` and `reasoning`), and `architecture`/modality — this is well-established public API shape, but I have no repo file enumerating those field names, so `unverified: the exact OpenRouter field names (context_length, pricing, supported_parameters) are not confirmed by a cited file in this evidence set`. Access is unauthenticated for the list, authenticated for inference; freshness is continuous (live endpoint). License: the model metadata is OpenRouter's own; per-model weights/licenses vary and are not carried in the list.

**LiteLLM cost map.** LiteLLM ships a static, versioned JSON cost map (`model_prices_and_context_window.json`) keyed by model name with `max_input_tokens`, `max_output_tokens`, `input_cost_per_token`, `output_cost_per_token`, `supports_function_calling`, `supports_reasoning`, etc. In this fleet LiteLLM is used as a router/proxy rather than as a catalog read: `atlas: /home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/DEVICE-BOOTSTRAP.md:324` documents the "LiteLLM router (`--with-litellm`, default **OFF**)" and `atlas: /home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/TODO-litellm.md:1` is the deferred TODO ("litellm (deferred, 2026-07-15)"). `atlas: /home/justin/nexus/nexus_cli/jarvis_brains.py:128` ("Cerebras via litellm proxy runner (free/fast)") confirms the proxy role. So the cost map is available but the fleet's usage is proxy routing, not schema ingestion. Freshness: updated per LiteLLM release (bundled file), so it lags new models by a release cycle. License: MIT (LiteLLM project) — `unverified: the MIT license claim for the LiteLLM cost map is not confirmed by a cited file here`.

**models.dev.** A community catalog (JSON/API) of providers and models with context limits, pricing, and capability flags, consumed by opencode and similar harnesses. I found no repo file referencing models.dev, so `unverified: models.dev's schema, update cadence, and license are not confirmed by any cited file or tool result in this evidence set`.

**Artificial Analysis.** Publishes model quality/speed/price indices (tokens/sec, time-to-first-token, blended $/M tokens) via a web dashboard and a paid/partner API. No repo reference found: `unverified: Artificial Analysis schema, access method, and license are not confirmed by any cited file here`.

**SWE-bench / Terminal-Bench.** These are evaluation harnesses, not model catalogs: SWE-bench ships task instances (repo, base commit, issue text, gold patch, test patch) as JSON/JSONL with a Docker-based evaluation runner; Terminal-Bench ships terminal task definitions with a containerized runner. They give pass-rate results, not per-model context/tool/reasoning metadata. No repo file in this evidence set references either benchmark, so `unverified: SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench dataset schemas, licenses, and update cadence are not confirmed by a cited file here`.

**What the fleet actually relies on.** The concrete, cited pattern is: OpenRouter's live model list as the capability/price source (`test_models_openrouter.py:54`, `test_proxy_openrouter.py:95`), LiteLLM as a routing proxy (`jarvis_brains.py:128`, `DEVICE-BOOTSTRAP.md:324`), and direct provider calls where the catalog lacks the model — `gnosis: transcript:nexus-brain:ab376a73-3982-4c38-9da6-9113cc35ab03:174` states "Firstmate calls Jev direct" precisely because OpenRouter's list had no Jev entry. That is the operational answer to "which catalog is authoritative": OpenRouter for anything it lists, direct provider APIs otherwise.

**Unknown:** the exact field-level schemas, update frequencies, and license terms for models.dev, Artificial Analysis, SWE-bench, and Terminal-Bench — no cited file or tool result in this evidence set describes them, and settling it would require reading each project's own schema/docs (e.g. a models.dev API response, the Artificial Analysis API docs, the SWE-bench dataset card, the Terminal-Bench task spec).

## 3. Benchmarks that evaluate harnesses (not just models)

The honest answer is that the field is thin here, and most of what is marketed as "harness benchmarking" is really model benchmarking run *through* a harness. The distinction matters for the nexus model picker.

**Benchmarks that are genuinely harness-sensitive (the harness is the variable):**

- **Terminal-Bench** — the closest thing to a harness benchmark. It scores an agent on end-to-end terminal tasks, so the score is a joint function of model *and* the agent loop/scaffold driving it. The same model under Claude Code vs. opencode vs. a bare loop produces different numbers. This is the one to watch for harness comparison.
- **SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified** — nominally a model benchmark, but published numbers are almost always "model X inside scaffold Y," and the scaffold is a large part of the delta. Treat leaderboard entries as harness+model pairs, not pure model capability.
- **Aider polyglot leaderboard** — same caveat: it is Aider's harness by construction, so it measures "model inside Aider," which is useful precisely because the harness is held fixed.
- **LMArena** — human-preference, chat-shaped, effectively harness-free (no tools, no loop). Not a harness benchmark.

I could not find a fleet artifact that enumerates these benchmarks or their harness-vs-model status. `unverified: the specific claim that Terminal-Bench is the only benchmark that varies the harness as a first-class axis` — this is my read of the public landscape, not something I can cite from the repo. The findings contain no benchmark catalog; the atlas hits are all OpenRouter/DeepSeek/LiteLLM plumbing (`/home/justin/gnosis/tests/test_proxy_openrouter.py:95`, `/home/justin/roundtable/roundtable/knowledge/providers.md:113`, `/home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/TODO-litellm.md:1`), not benchmark definitions.

## 4. What each harness needs (tools, plugins, MCP servers)

I have **no repo evidence** for a per-harness tool/plugin/MCP requirement matrix. Nothing in the findings describes Claude Code, opencode, Codex, Aider, OpenHands, or Cline's tool/plugin/MCP surface. So:

`unverified: the specific tools, plugins, or MCP servers each major harness (Claude Code, opencode, Codex, Aider, OpenHands, Cline) requires for coding, research, review, and one-shot jobs.` This is the single biggest gap in this sub-question and it needs a dedicated pass against each harness's own docs — it cannot be answered from the fleet index.

What I *can* ground from the fleet is the shape of the requirement in *our* stack, which is the relevant proxy:

- Harnesses in this fleet are wired through a **LiteLLM proxy** layer, and the proxy is the thing that carries provider routing. `nexus_cli/jarvis_brains.py:128` is documented as "Cerebras via litellm proxy runner (free/fast)" (`/home/justin/nexus/nexus_cli/jarvis_brains.py:128`), and the LiteLLM router is a device-bootstrap feature that is **default OFF** (`/home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/DEVICE-BOOTSTRAP.md:324`, `/home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/TODO-litellm.md:1`). So "what a harness needs" in our world is at minimum a reachable proxy endpoint plus a provider key.
- Provider keys are read per-provider: `read_deepseek_api_key` (`/home/justin/nexus/nexus_cli/deepseek_balance.py:19`), `openrouter_key` (`/home/justin/gnosis/tests/test_proxy_openrouter.py:95`), `deepseek_key` (`/home/justin/gnosis/tests/test_proxy_deepseek.py:97`). That is the concrete "what each job needs" surface we actually have.
- The hive itself is a LangGraph swarm (`D:\Dev\hive\README.md:1`, `D:\Dev\hive\langgraph.json:0` — keys `dependencies, graphs, checkpointer, env, http`), i.e. the orchestrator-plus-worker harness, and its closeout report is at `D:\Dev\hive\docs\langgraph-closeout-report-2026-09-03.md:1`.

## 5. The one harness-vs-model result the fleet *does* have

The most relevant measured harness result in the findings is the DeepSeek reviewer experiment inside the hive loop, which is a harness-level (not model-level) measurement:

- DeepSeek reviewer went from catching 5 of 19 defects to 18 of 19, but wrongly sent 8 of 16 good diffs back for fixes (was 2) — `transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:441`.
- Later: 15 of 19 caught, 7 of 16 good diffs sent back, one more than main — `transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:556`.
- Final: 15 of 19 caught, 5 of 16 good diffs sent back, all-model false-fix rate falls from 24 to 21 of 96 — `transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:684`.

That is a harness-configuration result (which reviewer model sits in which loop position), and it is the kind of measurement the nexus picker should be built to reproduce — not a public leaderboard.

## 6. Empirical data: direct single API calls vs. iterative agent harness loops

**What the evidence actually contains.** The findings for this sub-question are almost entirely about *which provider a model is routed through* (OpenRouter vs. direct, DeepSeek vs. Cerebras), not about a controlled comparison of one-shot calls against multi-turn agent loops. The closest thing to a measured harness-vs-harness result is a defect-detection comparison inside the hive swarm, not a direct-call-vs-loop comparison:

- gnosis transcript `.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:684` records a reviewer-model comparison: "DeepSeek now catches 15 of 19 and sends back 5 of 16 good diffs, against 6 of 16 on main. The all-model false-fix rate falls from 24 to 21 of 96." The same run at `:556` reports "15 of 19 caught and 7 of 16 good diffs sent back, one more than main," and at `:441` "DeepSeek now catches 18 of 19 defects (was 5), but it wrongly sends 8 of 16 good diffs back for fixes (was 2). That costs rounds." These are *reviewer-model* accuracy/false-positive numbers within an iterative loop — they quantify the cost of extra rounds ("That costs rounds") but they do not isolate loop overhead against a single call.
- gnosis transcript `.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:41` notes a LangGraph implementation detail ("LangGraph needs a Python-level reducer, not the builtin `max`"), which is about graph state plumbing, not call-vs-loop economics.

**Context-window inflation and token-cost overhead.** The one concrete measurement of per-call token accounting in the findings is gnosis transcript `.treehouse:0ba19423-c6cc-4721-a4d5-f1efbc4a8909:35`: "Now the probes: raw OpenRouter responses at a tiny max_tokens, plus what the stable (live) and worktree `_extract_usage` store." That is a probe of how usage fields are extracted from a single raw response — it establishes that usage is captured per call, but it does not measure how context grows across turns in a loop. No figure for context inflation (tokens added per iteration) or loop token-cost multiplier appears anywhere in the findings.

**Latency.** No latency comparison between a direct call and an agent loop appears in the findings. The only timing-adjacent facts are operational: gnosis transcript `nexus-brain:bf520a63-4df1-450d-88a1-8cdaa5282bc5:202` ("DeepSeek spend is down to about 1 cent an hour") and `nexus-brain:d8090af8-d67f-4f38-adb8-b06b0504291d:282` ("the one-hour check passed, so the background DeepSeek spend has stopped... The one DeepSeek call in that hour was..."). These are spend/rate observations, not latency.

**Task completion rates.** The defect-catch figures above (15/19, 18/19, 6/16, 8/16) are the only completion-style rates in the findings, and they measure a reviewer's classification accuracy, not whether a direct call or a loop completed a coding task.

**Routing facts that bear on the comparison but are not the comparison.** Several nodes establish that the fleet already mixes direct and gateway calls, which is the substrate any such experiment would run on: gnosis `nexus-brain:ab376a73-3982-4c38-9da6-9113cc35ab03:174` ("Jev is not on OpenRouter... Firstmate calls Jev direct"), `nexus-brain:62bc431d-a0b9-4f73-8d76-5f57779904c6:140` ("Jev is moving off Vercel to OpenRouter"), and `nexus-brain:ab376a73-3982-4c38-9da6-9113cc35ab03:173` ("jev is on openrouter isnt it?"). On the code side, atlas hits `nexus_cli/jarvis_brains.py:128` ("Cerebras via litellm proxy runner (free/fast)") and `nexus_cli/deepseek_balance.py:19` (`read_deepseek_api_key`) show direct-vs-proxy runners exist in nexus, but neither is a benchmark.

**Verdict.** The findings contain no controlled empirical study comparing direct single API calls against iterative agent harness loops on context inflation, token cost, latency, or task completion. What they do contain is (a) reviewer-model accuracy/false-positive counts inside the hive loop (gnosis `.treehouse:7362618c-...:684`, `:556`, `:441`), (b) a per-call usage-extraction probe (gnosis `.treehouse:0ba19423-...:35`), and (c) spend-rate observations (gnosis `nexus-brain:bf520a63-...:202`, `nexus-brain:d8090af8-...:282`).

**Unknown:** a direct-call-vs-loop benchmark with measured context inflation, token-cost multiplier, latency delta, and task-completion delta — none of the cited nodes report these, and no tool result in the findings supplies them. Such a measurement would settle the sub-question; the closest available proxy is the hive reviewer's round-cost data at gnosis `.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:441`/`:684`, which shows extra rounds cost accuracy trade-offs but does not price the loop against a single call.

## 7. Architecture and configuration changes for nexus's routing/fan-out setup

**1. Keep the classifier cheap and off the critical path — but verify its provider.** The evidence shows Jev's provider situation is unsettled: one transcript records "Jev is not on OpenRouter. OpenRouter's public model list has no Jev, typesafe or System One model, so our OpenRouter access doesn't cover it. Firstmate calls Jev direct" (gnosis transcript:nexus-brain:ab376a73-3982-4c38-9da6-9113cc35ab03:174), while a later one says "Jev is moving off Vercel to OpenRouter. A DeepSeek worker is building the change now" (gnosis transcript:nexus-brain:62bc431d-a0b9-4f73-8d76-5f57779904c6:140). Concrete change: pin Jev to a single documented route and record which one in config, so the classifier's latency/cost is a known quantity rather than a moving target. The industry pattern here is to keep the classifier as a small, fast, single-shot call (no agent loop) and reserve harness loops for the work itself.

**2. Make the free-model fan-out a tiered router, not a flat pool.** The evidence already contains a working precedent for tier mapping: `test_openrouter_gateway_maps_to_openrouter_tier` (atlas: /home/justin/vpsmate-home/projects/hive/tests/test_models_openrouter.py:54) and the `openrouter:{OPENROUTER_MODEL}` keying convention (atlas: /home/justin/vpsmate-home/projects/hive/tests/test_models_openrouter.py:0). Concrete change: route by job class — free models for high-volume, low-stakes fan-out (drafting, classification, first-pass review); paid Sonnet leads for the tasks that need tool-calling reliability and long context. This matches the observed cost discipline in the transcripts: "DeepSeek spend is down to about 1 cent an hour" (gnosis transcript:nexus-brain:bf520a63-4df1-450d-88a1-8cdaa5282bc5:202) and "the background DeepSeek spend has stopped" (gnosis transcript:nexus-brain:d8090af8-d67f-4f38-adb8-b06b0504291d:282) — i.e. the setup already benefits from explicitly bounding background spend.

**3. Tune the reviewer/verifier threshold rather than maximizing recall.** The hive transcripts give measured reviewer behavior: "DeepSeek now catches 18 of 19 defects (was 5), but it wrongly sends 8 of 16 good diffs back for fixes (was 2). That costs rounds" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:441), later "DeepSeek now catches 15 of 19 and sends back 5 of 16 good diffs, against 6 of 16 on main. The all-model false-fix rate falls from 24 to 21 of 96" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:684). Concrete change: treat the reviewer's false-positive rate as a first-class tuning target (it directly costs extra rounds), and keep the reviewer on a stronger model than the workers — the transcript records "the code reviewer now runs on Claude Sonnet" (gnosis transcript:nexus-brain:bf520a63-4df1-450d-88a1-8cdaa5282bc5:202). This is the standard asymmetric-verification pattern: cheap generation, stronger verification.

**4. Use a proxy/router layer for provider abstraction.** The evidence shows a litellm proxy runner already exists in nexus: "Cerebras via litellm proxy runner (free/fast)" (atlas: /home/justin/nexus/nexus_cli/jarvis_brains.py:128), and a deferred LiteLLM router in the device bootstrap (atlas: /home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/TODO-litellm.md:1; atlas: /home/justin/vps-config/device-bootstrap/DEVICE-BOOTSTRAP.md:324). Concrete change: put the free/paid model selection behind that router so switching a profile (free vs DeepSeek vs Sonnet) is a config change, not a code change — this is what makes the "free and DeepSeek profiles" in the LangGraph hive cheap to re-point.

**5. Keep the LangGraph hive's determinism and disjoint scopes.** The hive README describes the pattern: "A planner decomposes a spec into contract-first tasks with disjoint file scopes; workers build each task" (gnosis doc:hive:README.md). Concrete change: preserve disjoint file scopes when fanning out free models — parallel free-model workers on overlapping files is the main way fan-out loses to a single strong call. Note also the LangGraph reducer constraint: "LangGraph needs a Python-level reducer, not the builtin `max`" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:7362618c-cb61-4204-90c9-12f48a3291f5:41) — any new aggregation of fan-out results must use a named reducer.

**6. Bound context overhead by preferring direct calls for one-shot jobs.** The evidence includes a probe specifically measuring raw provider responses and stored usage: "the probes: raw OpenRouter responses at a tiny max_tokens, plus what the stable (live) and worktree `_extract_usage` store" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:0ba19423-c6cc-4721-a4d5-f1efbc4a8909:35). Concrete change: use that usage data to decide per job class whether a direct API call beats an agent loop — for one-shot classification/extraction, a direct call avoids the harness's system-prompt and tool-schema overhead.

**7. Respect the project's Python 3.10 / Windows constraints in any new routing module.** Any new module under `nexus_cli/` must be wired by name (import, registry entry, deploy/scripts reference, or `__main__` block) or `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py` fails, and TOML must be read the way `nexus_cli/account_registry.py` does (try `tomllib`, except `ModuleNotFoundError: import tomli as tomllib`). The evidence corroborates the 3.10 pathlib pitfall: "on 3.10 `Path.open` uses `pathlib._NormalAccessor.open`, which bypasses the patch" (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:636a2fb6-e9f2-4122-a453-dd3eb0db3fdd:345). Concrete change: if the router reads a model catalog from TOML, use the account_registry fallback pattern and test with `tmp_path`, not POSIX-only tricks.

**Unknown:** the specific measured context-overhead and cost numbers for direct-call vs harness on nexus's own workloads — the `_extract_usage` probe (gnosis transcript:.treehouse:0ba19423-c6cc-4721-a4d5-f1efbc4a8909:35) is referenced but its results are not in the findings, and that data would settle which job classes should bypass the harness. Also unknown: the current authoritative Jev route (the two transcripts conflict), which would settle whether the classifier is on OpenRouter or direct.

## 8. External guidance on supervisor-worker efficiency

The web-search findings on orchestrator-worker patterns are attributed only to opaque `vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/...` redirect links, not to the underlying source URLs. The named sources in the Sources block (beam.ai, glukhov.org, tianpan.co, reddit.com, towardsai.net, redis.io, arize.com, splunk.com, overpayingforai.com, zaun.ai, youtube.com, arxiv.org, medium.com, mit.edu) are listed by domain only, with the redirect URL as the link target — the actual article URLs are not present in the findings. Because the underlying source URLs are not resolvable from the findings, the following external claims are marked **`unsupported`** rather than presented as grounded fact:

- `unsupported`: that orchestrator-worker patterns "frequently fail due to context window saturation and misclassification" (attributed to beam.ai / glukhov.org via redirect links).
- `unsupported`: that passing a massive tool namespace directly to an LLM degrades performance, and that intent-based routing should provide a curated tool subset (attributed to tianpan.co via a redirect link).
- `unsupported`: that simple tasks (single file reads, small grep operations) should bypass the agent loop entirely, and that direct API calls for trivial tasks avoid supervisor-worker coordination latency/cost (attributed to reddit.com / towardsai.net / redis.io via redirect links).
- `unsupported`: that state management should be externalized (Redis or persistent check-pointing) to prevent the supervisor becoming a bottleneck (attributed to arize.com / glukhov.org via redirect links).
- `unsupported`: that escalation rules (promote to a more expensive model only after a cheaper model fails) are more efficient than per-sub-task supervisor guessing (attributed to splunk.com / overpayingforai.com / zaun.ai via redirect links).
- `unsupported`: that context compaction (summarizing/pruning history before passing to the next agent) mitigates agent-loop token costs (attributed to reddit.com via a redirect link).
- `unsupported`: that tracking cheap-model rejection rates and adjusting routing logic accordingly is a recommended practice (attributed to splunk.com / overpayingforai.com / youtube.com via redirect links).
- `unsupported`: that Jev should be fine-tuned to predict cost-performance efficiency of candidate models (attributed to arxiv.org via a redirect link).
- `unsupported`: that scripted hooks should replace soft prompt-based rules for governance (attributed to medium.com via a redirect link).
- `unsupported`: that an "Ideal Router" (Oracle) baseline should be used to measure classifier gap (attributed to mit.edu via a redirect link).

These are directionally consistent with the internal evidence in §7 (cheap classifier, tiered routing, escalation, context bounding), but they cannot be cited as external fact until the real source URLs are retrieved. The internal evidence in §7 stands on its own gnosis/atlas citations and does not depend on these external claims.

## Build first

1. **Pin Jev's route in config and record it.** The two transcripts conflict on whether Jev is direct or on OpenRouter (gnosis `nexus-brain:ab376a73-...:174` vs `nexus-brain:62bc431d-...:140`). Resolve to one documented route so the classifier's latency/cost is a known quantity. This is the smallest change with the largest effect on routing predictability.
2. **Add a tiered router keyed by job class, reusing the existing `openrouter:{MODEL}` convention** (`test_models_openrouter.py:0`, `:54`). Free models for high-volume fan-out; paid Sonnet for tool-calling/long-context work. Put the selection behind the existing litellm proxy runner (`nexus_cli/jarvis_brains.py:128`) so profile switches are config, not code.
3. **Instrument the reviewer's false-positive rate as a first-class metric.** The hive data already shows the tradeoff (gnosis `.treehouse:7362618c-...:441`, `:684`): catching more defects cost extra rounds. Track false-rejects per reviewer model and tune the threshold rather than maximizing recall.
4. **Wire any new `nexus_cli/` routing module in the same task that creates it** — import, registry entry, deploy/scripts reference, or `__main__` block — or `tests/test_orphan_ratchet.py` fails. Read TOML via the `nexus_cli/account_registry.py` fallback (`try tomllib / except ModuleNotFoundError: import tomli as tomllib`), and write tests with `tmp_path` and no POSIX-only tricks (Windows + Python 3.10 pre-push gate).
5. **Run the direct-call-vs-loop measurement the findings lack.** The `_extract_usage` probe (gnosis `.treehouse:0ba19423-...:35`) already captures per-call usage; extend it to compare a one-shot call against the harness loop on the same job class, measuring context inflation, token cost, and latency. That data settles which job classes should bypass the harness — currently **unknown**.
